Dromore
druh-more'
n. (the small County Down see, left nearly empty for most of the Reformation century)
From Irish Droim Mor, the great ridge; droim, a ridge or back, and mor, great.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dromore was the smallest of the Ulster sees, a poor diocese in County Down. Through most of the Reformation century it was held in commendam by bishops of other dioceses, left vacant, or given to men who did not reside; the cathedral was a ruin, the parish churches mostly roofless, and the revenues alienated into lay hands before any of the reforming bishops arrived. Jeremy Taylor, bishop from 1661, found a diocese with almost no working ministry and rebuilt the cathedral out of his own means. The dictionary records Dromore not for an event but for an absence, which is the commonest way a church dies: no one does anything to it. Ezekiel puts the charge against shepherds entirely in terms of things not done: “neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines commendam as the holding of a benefice in trust until a pastor is provided; to alienate as to transfer title or property to another; and diligent as steady in application, assiduous.

expand to see more

COMMENDAM, n. [L.] A benefice or living commended, by the void of a pastor, to the care of a clerk until a regular incumbent is provided.

ALIENATE, v.t. [L. alieno.] To transfer title or property to another; to estrange; to withdraw affection.

DILIGENT, a. [L. diligens.] Steady in application to business; constant in effort; assiduous; attentive.

VACANT, a. [L. vacans.] Empty; not filled; unoccupied with an incumbent or possessor.

IDOL, a. [Gr. eidolon.] An image; in Scripture also used of that which is worthless or good for nothing.

Key Scripture

Eze 34:4 — "The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them."

Eze 34:6 — "My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and upon every high hill: yea, my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth, and none did search or seek after them."

Pro 27:23 — "Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds."

Zec 11:17 — "Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened."

Modern Corruption

The smallest Ulster see, held in commendam or left vacant through most of the Reformation century, with a ruined cathedral and alienated revenues.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Dromore is where the dictionary has to say something uncomfortable about its own tradition's record. There is a great deal of writing about Irish resistance to the Reformation and much less about dioceses where the Reformation never actually arrived to be resisted. A see with no resident bishop, no repaired churches, no catechising and no revenue left to pay a minister with had not been rejected by the people of County Down. It had been abandoned by the church that claimed it.

The principle to recover is that the shepherd's sin in Scripture is most often an omission, and that Ezekiel's indictment against the shepherds of Israel is a list of things left undone. Five clauses in a row say what was not done, beginning “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick” (Eze 34:4), and the last of them is the plainest: “neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4). The consequence follows as night follows a shut door: “My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and upon every high hill” (Eze 34:6), and the chapter adds that “none did search or seek after them” (Eze 34:6). Proverbs states the positive duty as personal attention — “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23) — and Zechariah pronounces woe on the shepherd who simply leaves (Zec 11:17).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew baqash (H1245), to seek or search for; Hebrew 'abad (H6), to be lost or perish.

expand to see more

Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, to search out; “neither have ye sought that which was lost”, Ezekiel 34:4.

Hebrew 'abad (H6) — to perish, to be lost; Ezekiel 34:4.

Hebrew darash (H1875) — to search, to inquire after; “none did search or seek after them”, Ezekiel 34:6.

Hebrew yada' (H3045) — to know, to perceive; “to know the state of thy flocks”, Proverbs 27:23.

Hebrew 'eliyl (H457) — worthless, good for nothing, an idol; “the idol shepherd”, Zechariah 11:17.

Usage

"“neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4) — held in commendam or left vacant for most of a century."

"“and none did search or seek after them” (Eze 34:6) — the cathedral a ruin and the parish churches roofless."

"“Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23) — Jeremy Taylor rebuilt the cathedral from his own means after 1661."
